tagline.text: Palawan's highest peak and the Philippines' toughest trek through indigenous villages

location.label: Location
location.text: Mantalingahan Protected Landscape, around Brooke's Point and Rizal, southern Palawan

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~4,000 (for a team of five, from Puerto Princesa)

children.text: Mount Mantalingahan rises 2,086 m above sea level and is the highest peak on Palawan. It stands at the heart of a 120,457-hectare protected landscape, and the trek, which starts at Ransang village in Rizal and passes indigenous villages, mossy forest and a knife-edge ridge, is known as a demanding 4–5 day climb.
Mount Mantalingahan (
Mount Mantalingahan
, also spelled Mantalingajan) is a mountain in the Brooke's Point area of southern Palawan. At

it is the highest point on Palawan, and Wikipedia describes it as the 68th-highest island peak in the world and the 10th most prominent mountain in the Philippines. Its coordinates are roughly 8°49′ N, 117°40′ E.

The mountain is the center of the Mount Mantalingahan Protected Landscape, which covers 1,204.57 km² (120,457 hectares). It was proclaimed on June 23, 2009 under Proclamation No. 1815, and the whole range is protected as a national park. The protected landscape is on the tentative list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and the nomination process was reportedly formally started in May 2018. The Indigenous Palawan people known as the Tau't Bato live around the mountain.

The mountain is the highest part of the Beaufort Mountains, an area of ultramafic rock formed in the Eocene. New plants and animals are still being discovered here: the pitcher plant Nepenthes mantalingajanensis, reported in 2007, is named after the mountain, and a new beetle and a shrew have also been reported. The area continues to face pressure from logging and mining.

The climb is rated 9 out of 9 for difficulty on the Philippine hiking site PinoyMountaineer, which also says it cannot be done as a day hike. Access from Manila or Puerto Princesa is not easy either, so this is a destination for well-prepared trekkers, not a general sightseeing spot. This guide is based on Wikipedia and two hiking sites; many of the fee and permit records are old, so please be sure to check the latest information. Counting travel days, the schedule easily runs beyond six days, so plan your flights with room to spare.
The summit is
above sea level. One record says the true highest point lies about
2km
north along the summit ridge, separate from the southern top that most people climb. The two trails are also recorded as meeting at a point about 1,600 m above sea level, west of the ridge.
Near the summit a narrow ridge (the Knife Edge) and a canopy section through the treetops follow one after another. Gloves are advised for the summit assault.
The trail passes villages and campsites of the Indigenous Tau't Bato people of Palawan. Some residents are wary of catching colds from outsiders, so it is best to be polite and keep your distance.
You can see unusual vegetation growing on the Beaufort ultramafic rock. The pitcher plant Nepenthes mantalingajanensis is a species named after this mountain.
Streams near campsites such as Balin-Balin, Kabugan and Paray-Paray make it relatively easy to get drinking water. The last water source is at the Palay-Palay campsite.

The usual route climbs from Ransang and comes down on the other side at Malis village in Brooke's Point. It is described as a 4-day guided traverse, while Wikipedia mentions three days up and two days down.

children.text: Travel from Puerto Princesa to Rizal and stay overnight. Buy food at the market, pay a courtesy call at the municipal and tourism offices, and check the climb registration logbooks.
Start walking at Ransang village, pass Balin-Balin and the next village, and look for a guide and porters. After crossing four brooks you reach the Balu'in campsite around
Pass the Kawayan campsite and Agong-Agungan; the canopy walk begins on Mt. Tulanggok. Spend the night at the Palay-Palay campsite.
Leave around
with a packed lunch, pass Simba Rock and the first peak at 2,055 m, and reach the summit around
. Come down early in the afternoon and return to Palay-Palay.

Pass Balin-Balin, descend to the starting point and return to Puerto Princesa.
These times are for reference only, based on 2008 records. Depending on your fitness and the weather, each day may run longer, so keep spare days.

items.title: 4-day guided traverse
items.subtitle: From Ransang all the way to Malis

children.text: Walk from Ransang (about 30 m above sea level) to the Magtangob or Balin-Balin campsite.
Climb to the Paray-Paray campsite. The forest around here is a mossy, swamp-like jungle.
Cross the knife-edge canopy section, climb to the summit, and then descend toward Brooke's Point.
Come out at Malis village (about 40 m above sea level), close to the southeastern coast. From Malis you can take a van to Puerto Princesa.

The distance and walking time for each day are not given in the sources, so decide them with a local guide. Some accounts, including Wikipedia, also describe three days up and two days down, so it is safer to add spare days to match your team's pace.
There are several flights a day from Manila (MNL) to Puerto Princesa (PPS). Check the number of flights and times with the airlines.
From Puerto Princesa airport, take a tricycle to the city bus terminal or the San Jose terminal.
Southern Palawan is a long way from Manila, so flying into Puerto Princesa is the usual way to go. This guide has no information on an overland route from Manila.

Charing Bus Lines runs to Rizal. In past records the fare is about ₱250, and a booking portal updated in September 2026 lists Cherry Bus leaving the New Central Bus Terminal at 11:30 and 12:30 for ₱325 regular aircon (possibly higher with fuel surcharges).
Vans also leave the San Jose terminal several times a day, at about ₱300 in past records, with the last departure reported around
The trip takes about
4~5 hours
Fares and last-departure times may change, so check at the terminal yourself.
A motorcycle ride (habal-habal) costs about ₱400 per person in past records.
For a large group, renting a jeepney is the better choice.
From Malis village, vans to Puerto Princesa run between
and
, at about ₱300 in past records.
A slower roll-on roll-off (RORO) bus is also available.
The safest months for the climb are the dry season from December to May. Afternoon rain makes the rocky sections slippery, so it is best to come down early from the summit.
June to August is the rainy season, and the trails are said to become almost impassable. Avoid entering the mountain at this time, and check the latest permit situation in particular.

Most people stay at a small lodge in Rizal before and after the climb, and past records mention a room at about ₱150 a night. If you want more comforts, stay in Puerto Princesa city and set out a day earlier. On the mountain, your lodging is campsites and village huts.

There are no restaurants on the mountain, so buy plenty of food at the Rizal market in advance. You will need packed lunches for summit day, and you should count the meals of your guide and porters too. When you sleep in village huts, use a mosquito net and respect the villagers' rules.

After the traverse, when you come out at Malis village, you can take a van toward Puerto Princesa from the Brooke's Point side. Back in Puerto Princesa, recover with seafood and Filipino dishes at a restaurant in town. Before the climb, buying rice, canned food, dried fish, coffee and snacks at the market makes cooking at the campsites easier. Guides and porters usually cook rice in the local way, but confirm the amounts beforehand.

Before entering the mountain, you must sign the logbooks and pay the required fees at the Rizal tourism office, the police station, the DENR-CENRO in Quezon, and Ransang village. Procedures may change, so check the latest notices.
Guides and porters cost about ₱500 per day, and it is best to have them for the whole trip. Also budget for the guide's transport back to Rizal.
Carrying a full pack to the summit is nearly impossible, so leave your gear at the Palay-Palay campsite and climb light.
Gloves are needed for the summit assault. There are no roped sections, but some stretches may require help.
Mobile signal can be picked up in many places, and it is stronger on the Brooke's Point side. A 3G signal from Globe and Smart has been recorded at Paray-Paray, but it is not guaranteed.
Some streams are regarded as taboo and must not be drunk from. Follow your guide's instructions.
Leeches (limatik) appear only in some stretches, in small numbers or mildly, and there are rattan and thorny plants, so wear long clothing.
The Rizal area is known to be malaria-endemic, so check with a medical provider and the latest prevention guidance before you go.
Bring a waterproof pack cover, dry clothes to change into, a headlamp, water purification gear, gloves and long trousers. Rain is frequent, so put all your belongings in waterproof bags.
Allow at least six days for the trip, including travel days and spare days, and book your return flight with room to spare.
Mount Mantalingahan is a remote area counted among the most difficult hikes in the Philippines. Do not climb alone or enter the mountain without a permit.
It is a 4–6 day trip that cannot be done in a day. Do not attempt it without fitness and camping experience.
Moving after dark is not recommended because of snakes, and avoid leaving the trail.
Afternoon rain makes the rocky sections dangerous. Come down early from the summit.
In indigenous villages, ask the residents first about taking photos and making contact, and respect their culture.
Many of the fees and contacts in this guide are based on 2008 records and a 2014 update. Check the latest fees, permits and contacts with the DENR and tourism offices.
